text.text: <atomic>Matt plays for his local football team.</atomic>
<atomic>He was curious how the different positions he plays affect his average heart rate.</atomic>
<atomic>He believed that since he ran longer distances on defense, his average heart rate would be higher when playing defensive positions.</atomic>
<atomic>For several weeks, Matt tracked his heart rate and the positions he played.</atomic>
<atomic>He discovered that his average heart rate when playing on offense, at 124 beats per minute, was higher than his average heart rate when playing on defense, at 115 beats per minute.</atomic>
<atomic>Based on his results, Matt thought that perhaps his average heart rate was higher on offense because he moved more quickly in those positions.</atomic>

pieces.text: Scientists use observations and background knowledge to pose a question about a scientific problem.

Scientists examine their data for trends and patterns, often using charts, graphs, or tables.
Scientists determine whether their data supports their hypothesis. If their hypothesis was not supported, they may
by making a new prediction.

imageLabel.text: a Petri dish with clusters of bacteria

text.text: <atomic>Ava's friends followed the "five-second rule": they would eat food that had dropped on the floor, but only if it was on the floor for less than five seconds.</atomic>
<atomic>Ava thought that bacteria would stick to food as soon as it touched the floor, so the amount of time on the floor wouldn't affect how much bacteria stuck to the food.</atomic>

<atomic>She placed twelve boiled noodles on the kitchen floor, picked up six after three seconds, and picked up the rest after ten seconds. Then, she touched each noodle to a separate Petri dish used to grow bacteria.</atomic>
<atomic>After one week, the bacteria that had transferred from each noodle to its Petri dish had grown to visible clusters.</atomic>

<atomic>Because there were more bacteria on the ten-second dishes than the three-second dishes, Ava reasoned that the amount of time on the floor did affect how much bacteria stuck to the food.</atomic>
<atomic>She showed her friends pictures of the Petri dishes and a graph of her results.</atomic>

text.text: <atomic>Nick grows basil plants in pots on his back porch. He noticed that his basil plants did not grow many leaves.</atomic>
<atomic>He read in a book that earthworms in the soil have helped parsley plants grow.</atomic>
<atomic>This made him consider whether his basil plants were not growing many leaves because their soil lacked earthworms, and whether his plants would grow more leaves if he added some.</atomic>
<atomic>Nick added earthworms to the soil in five of his ten pots. After two months of growth, he counted the number of leaves on all ten plants.</atomic>
<atomic>He found that, on average, the plants with earthworms had 64 leaves, while the plants without earthworms had 51 leaves.</atomic>
<atomic>Nick shared the results of his experiment with his neighbors.</atomic>

text.text: <atomic>Logan took his motorized toy boat to the park with his cousin.</atomic>
<atomic>The boat zipped across the pond, and Logan wondered if adding mass to the boat would affect its speed.</atomic>
<atomic>He didn't think so, since the motor should keep propelling it at the same rate.</atomic>

<atomic>Logan decided to time the boat as it traveled from one side of the pond to the other. He then taped a pebble to the boat and timed it again. Finally, he added a second pebble and repeated the procedure.</atomic>
<atomic>Logan noticed that as he added mass, the trips took longer. The empty boat took the least time to cross the pond, and the boat with two pebbles took the longest.</atomic>
<atomic>Logan concluded that adding mass does slow down the boat.</atomic>
<atomic>He changed his prediction: The motor must provide a set amount of force, so it can't maintain the same speed as more mass is added.</atomic>
<atomic>He shared his results with his aunt and confirmed that the boat's motor exerts a consistent force, so increasing the boat's mass reduces its acceleration.</atomic>

text.text: <atomic>One summer day, Christy was outside helping her dad spray paint some handles for their kitchen cabinets. When they finished, her dad asked her to take the spray paint inside, because leaving it in the hot sun could cause the canisters to explode. He explained that raising a gas's temperature also raises its pressure. Christy wondered how she could test this relationship.</atomic>
<atomic>Not wanting to cause any explosions, she decided to test it with her dad's car tires.</atomic>
<atomic>She predicted that the tire pressure would increase after he drove, since the tires would warm up on the road.</atomic>
<atomic>She measured the pressure of each tire on her dad's car before he drove it to work. When he came home, she measured the pressure again.</atomic>
<atomic>She was excited to see that each tire's pressure had increased!</atomic>
<atomic>She concluded that she was correct in predicting that driving raises the pressure in car tires.</atomic>

text.text: <atomic>Lester had a hydrangea plant that produced blue flowers. He moved his plant from a pot to a planter bed in his yard, and the next time the plant flowered, the flowers were pink!</atomic>
<atomic>He tested the soils and found that the pH, or acidity, differed between the pot and the planter bed.</atomic>
<atomic>This led him to wonder if soil pH could affect the color of hydrangea flowers.</atomic>
<atomic>Lester filled five pots with soil with a pH of 5.0 and another five with soil with a pH of 6.5. He planted six hydrangea seeds in each pot.</atomic>
<atomic>He found that the plants grown in pH 6.5 soil bloomed pink, while those grown in pH 5.0 soil bloomed blue.</atomic>
<atomic>Lester deduced that soil pH influences hydrangea flower color.</atomic>
<atomic>He shared his results on his favorite gardening blog.</atomic>

<atomic>He knew that during activation, yeast turns carbohydrates and oxygen into carbon dioxide. So, he predicted that adding more sugar would cause the yeast to bubble more.</atomic>
<atomic>Tony activated two batches of yeast: one with 100℉ water and 1 teaspoon of sugar, and the other with 100℉ water and 2 teaspoons of sugar.</atomic>
<atomic>After letting each batch sit for 15 minutes, he discovered that both were bubbling the same amount.</atomic>
<atomic>He concluded that both batches had enough sugar to allow the yeast to create carbon dioxide, so adding more sugar did not impact the process.</atomic>
<atomic>Tony then predicted that using higher-temperature water during activation would cause the yeast to bubble more.</atomic>

text.text: <atomic>While washing his hands at his aunt's house, Malik noticed that the soap didn't seem to lather as much as it did at his own house.</atomic>
<atomic>He remembered hearing that "hard water" has a higher mineral content than "soft water."</atomic>
<atomic>He wondered if the soap lathered less at his aunt's house due to the water having a higher mineral content.</atomic>

<atomic>When he got home, Malik filled 12 identical bottles with the same volume of distilled water. He added nothing to 4 of the bottles, one teaspoon of Epsom salt to 4 of the bottles, and two teaspoons of Epsom salt to the remaining 4 bottles. After adding a drop of soap to the first bottle, he put his thumb over the opening and shook it to make bubbles. He then used a ruler to measure the height of the bubbles.</atomic>

<atomic>Once he had repeated the procedure with all of the bottles, Malik calculated the average height of the bubbles for each type of water. He found that the bottles containing only distilled water had the tallest column of bubbles, and the bottles with two teaspoons of Epsom salt added had the shortest.</atomic>
<atomic>He concluded that soap lathers less in hard water than it does in soft water.</atomic>
<atomic>When Malik told his aunt about the experiment, she confirmed that her house does have hard water.</atomic>

text.text: <atomic>Pete grows tomato plants in his garden. Recently, deer have come into his garden to eat his tomato plants.</atomic>
<atomic>He read that deer do not like garlic and wondered if he could use garlic to stop deer from eating his tomato plants.</atomic>
<atomic>He predicted that spraying his tomato plants with garlic water would stop the deer from eating them.</atomic>
<atomic>Pete sprayed half of his tomato plants with garlic water and left the other half unsprayed. He recorded which plants the deer ate every day for two weeks.</atomic>
<atomic>He found that the deer avoided the tomato plants sprayed with garlic water but continued to eat the unsprayed plants.</atomic>
<atomic>Pete concluded that garlic water can be used to repel deer from tomato plants.</atomic>
<atomic>He shared his findings with his gardening club.</atomic>

text.text: <atomic>Sue watched boats on the river.</atomic>
<atomic>She noticed that some of the boats were V-shaped, and other boats seemed to have flat bottoms.</atomic>
<atomic>She speculated that the shape of the boat bottom might affect how much weight the boat could hold, so that flat-bottomed boats would hold more weight.</atomic>
<atomic>So, she decided to make several aluminum foil boats to float in the bathtub.</atomic>
<atomic>She made ten boats with flat bottoms and ten boats with V-shaped bottoms, and then she kept track of the number of pennies it took to sink each boat in the water.</atomic>
<atomic>Sue compared the average number of pennies it took to sink the boats in each of the two groups.</atomic>
<atomic>Because the flat-bottomed boats held more pennies, she reasoned that the shape of the boat bottom affected how much weight the boat could hold.</atomic>

text.text: <atomic>Jen bakes bread for a bakery. She stores her bread in clear bins in the back of the bakery, but she sometimes finds mold growing on the bread.</atomic>
<atomic>She wanted to know if exposure to light affects mold growth.</atomic>
<atomic>She predicted that less mold would grow on her bread if she stored it in dark bins.</atomic>
<atomic>For two weeks, Jen stored half of her bread in dark bins and the other half in clear bins.</atomic>
<atomic>She found that the same amount of mold grew on bread in both types of bins. She also noticed that bread in bins stored closer to the oven had the most mold.</atomic>
<atomic>Based on her experiment, Jen determined that light did not have a major effect on the total amount of mold that grew on her bread.</atomic>
<atomic>She thought that temperature might affect mold growth and that less mold would grow on bread stored in cold conditions.</atomic>

text.text: <atomic>Alvin was helping his mom make pickles. As he was adding salt to water to make brine, he recalled that sugar dissolves better in hot water than in cold.</atomic>
<atomic>Alvin thought that the temperature of the water might also affect how well salt would dissolve.</atomic>

<atomic>To test this idea, Alvin filled nine identical glasses with equal volumes of water. He filled three with water that was heated on the stovetop, three with water at room temperature, and the remaining three with chilled water. Then he added a tablespoon of salt to each glass and stirred the water. Alvin continued to add one tablespoon at a time to each glass until the salt no longer dissolved.</atomic>

<atomic>He calculated the average amount of dissolved salt for each group. He found that the glasses containing chilled water dissolved the least amount of salt, and the glasses containing hot water dissolved the most.</atomic>
<atomic>He concluded that the temperature of the water does indeed affect the solubility of salt.</atomic>
<atomic>He asked his mom why this was the case, and she explained that the warmer water molecules move faster, which helps them break apart the salt crystals.</atomic>

<atomic>She wondered if adding a nitrogen-based fertilizer to the soil would increase the growth rate of her herbs.</atomic>
<atomic>Sofia added a nitrogen-based fertilizer to the soil of half the herbs and left the other half unchanged. After one month, she measured the height of all of the herbs.</atomic>
<atomic>She found that the herbs without fertilizer grew to an average height of 6 inches, while the herbs with fertilizer grew to an average height of 10 inches.</atomic>
<atomic>Sofia concluded that nitrogen-based fertilizer increases the rate at which herbs grow.</atomic>
<atomic>Sofia shared her findings with her colleagues at the community garden.</atomic>

text.text: <atomic>Mary recently heard about acupressure mats, which are covered in small plastic spikes. Mary was surprised to learn that people find these mats comfortable—and even therapeutic.</atomic>
<atomic>She guessed that spreading a person's weight over a large number of spikes would decrease the pressure exerted by each spike.</atomic>

<atomic>Mary collected three identical balloons, some nails, three wooden boards, and a textbook. She then hammered one nail through the first board, nine nails in a grid measuring three inches by three inches through the second, and 36 nails in a grid of the same size through the last. Mary held the first balloon on the single nail and placed the textbook on top. The balloon popped instantly, suggesting that the nail exerted a lot of pressure. She held the next balloon on the grid of nine nails and placed the textbook on top. This time, the balloon took a moment to pop. Finally, Mary repeated the procedure with the 36-nail grid, and the balloon did not pop at all!</atomic>
<atomic>Mary determined that when weight is distributed over many spikes—like on an acupressure mat—each spike exerts only a small amount of pressure.</atomic>

text.text: <atomic>After walking by some rusted cars parked in the street, Susan wondered whether all metals are equally susceptible to corrosion.</atomic>
<atomic>Susan could not recall ever seeing rusted aluminum objects, and she reasoned that aluminum must be less susceptible to corrosion than other metals, like iron.</atomic>

<atomic>Susan gathered some iron nails and aluminum foil. She prepared a saline solution by mixing salt into water. She then poured equal amounts of the solution into four separate cups. Next, she placed an iron nail in two of the cups and a piece of aluminum foil in the other two.</atomic>
<atomic>By the end of the week, Susan noticed that the iron nails had rusted significantly, while the aluminum foil showed almost no signs of corrosion.</atomic>
<atomic>She determined that iron is highly susceptible to corrosion in saline conditions, while aluminum is much more resistant.</atomic>

text.text: <atomic>Katie watched her sister change a tire. One bolt seemed stuck, so she took a hollow pipe and put it over the wrench's handle to make it longer.</atomic>
<atomic>Katie wondered why this helped her sister remove the bolts.</atomic>
<atomic>She predicted that the longer handle allows a person to use less force to turn the wrench.</atomic>

<atomic>To test her idea, Katie and her sister drilled nine small bolts into a wooden board. Katie then attached a spring scale to a normal wrench. As she pulled the spring scale at a right angle to turn the wrench, she measured the force it took to remove a bolt. She repeated this with two more bolts and averaged the three measurements. Then she put a short pipe over the handle and removed the next three bolts. Finally, she put a long pipe over the handle and repeated the procedure.</atomic>
<atomic>When she compared the three averages, she found that the longest handle took the least force to remove the bolts, while the unmodified wrench took the most.</atomic>
<atomic>Katie concluded that the longer a wrench's handle is, the less force it takes to turn it.</atomic>

<atomic>He had heard that sand, when heated by the sun, could melt ice.</atomic>

<atomic>He sprinkled sand on half the ice cubes and left the other half unsanded.</atomic>
<atomic>He placed all the cubes outside for one hour and then brushed off the sand and reweighed them.</atomic>
<atomic>Ed calculated the average weight of each type of cube to see if the sanded cubes melted more than the unsanded cubes.</atomic>
<atomic>He decided that sand did not speed up melting, since the two types of ice cubes were similar weights.</atomic>
<atomic>Then, he read that salt makes ice melt at a cooler temperature.</atomic>
<atomic>He predicted that because the melting temperature would be lowered, ice cubes would melt faster if he applied salt to them.</atomic>

text.text: <atomic>Stacy bought fruit at the grocery store. She placed some of the fruit in her lunchbox and the rest on the counter.</atomic>
<atomic>The next day, she noticed that the fruit in her lunchbox had ripened more than the fruit on the counter.</atomic>
<atomic>She wondered if fruit ripened faster when in a closed container.</atomic>
<atomic>Stacy predicted that fruit in a closed container would ripen faster than fruit left in the open.</atomic>

<atomic>She found that the banana in the box had ripened more than the banana left on the counter.</atomic>
<atomic>Stacy concluded that fruit in closed containers ripens faster than fruit left out in the open.</atomic>
<atomic>She shared what she found with her friends and family.</atomic>

<atomic>He read that flowers grow better in slightly acidic soil, so he wondered if adding vinegar would help his flowers grow.</atomic>
<atomic>He predicted that since vinegar is acidic, mixing it with the water when watering his flowers would make them grow larger.</atomic>
<atomic>Mike planted identical flowers in two pots. For one month he watered one pot with water and the other with a mixture of water and vinegar.</atomic>
<atomic>He found that the flowers he watered with water alone grew well, while those watered with vinegar and water wilted.</atomic>
<atomic>Mike concluded that the vinegar damaged the flowers it came into direct contact with.</atomic>
<atomic>He then predicted that lowering the pH of the soil by adding aluminum sulfate would improve the growth of his flowers.</atomic>

text.text: <atomic>To introduce color theory, Cody's science teacher gave each lab group three colored bulbs: one blue, one green, and one red. She instructed the groups to predict what colors the bulbs' lights would make when mixed.</atomic>

<atomic>Cody's group reasoned that the colors should mix just like paint—red and green would make brown, blue and red would make purple, blue and green would make teal, and all three would make a dark brownish color.</atomic>
<atomic>To test their predictions, Cody and his group shined their bulbs on the wall so that the colored light overlapped.</atomic>
<atomic>The resulting colors were not what the group had expected. Red and green made yellow, blue and green made cyan, blue and red made magenta, and all three made white!</atomic>
<atomic>They decided that they were wrong, and that colored bulbs must be different from paint.</atomic>
<atomic>All the groups shared their results, and their teacher explained that paint absorbs certain colors of light and reflects others, while bulbs produce certain colors of light.</atomic>

text.text: <atomic>Mark grows orchids in his home.</atomic>
<atomic>He wondered if the color of light the orchids received could impact how well they grew.</atomic>
<atomic>He predicted that since the orchids' leaves are green, green light would make them grow the tallest.</atomic>

<atomic>Mark planted three orchids in the same conditions. Once they sprouted, he placed each orchid in a separate dark room and provided each with eight hours of red, green, or blue light. He then measured the growth of each orchid over time.</atomic>
<atomic>He discovered that the orchid with red light grew to 24 inches, the orchid with blue light grew to 20 inches, and the orchid with green light grew to 18 inches.</atomic>
<atomic>Based on his findings, Mark determined that green light did not produce the tallest growth.</atomic>

<atomic>After conducting more research, he predicted that green light made the orchid grow the least because the orchid's green leaves reflect the green light instead of absorbing it for energy.</atomic>

alternativeText.text: a fire burning through a prairie

elements.text: Dr. King was the land manager for a prairie that had become overrun by unwanted grasses. These grasses crowded out other plants. Dr. King thought that she could use fire to remove the unwanted grasses and allow other plants to grow. But she didn't know how often the prairie should be burned.

Dr. King marked off six plots within a large area of the prairie. She used carefully controlled fires to burn all of the plants in each plot. She burned three of the plots once a year for three years. She burned the other three plots twice a year for three years. A year after the last fire, Dr. King counted the number of unwanted grasses in each of the six plots.

alternativeText.text: a person picking blackberries from a bush

elements.text: Jamal's grandmother suggested that soaking berries in hot water might help prevent the berries from getting moldy.

To test this idea, Jamal harvested fresh blackberries and divided them evenly into eight bowls. He filled four of the bowls with room temperature water and the other four bowls with water heated to 125°F. Jamal let all of the berries soak in the water for 30 seconds. Then, he poured out the water and dried the berries. Jamal placed the two groups of bowls in the refrigerator, keeping each group separate. After five days, Jamal counted the number of moldy blackberries in each bowl.

elements.text: Many types of bacteria cannot survive on objects made of copper. Dr. West was considering using beds with copper bed rails instead of beds with plastic rails at the hospital where she worked. She wanted to know if copper bed rails would reduce the number of patients who got new infections.

To test this, Dr. West had beds with copper rails placed in half of the hospital rooms. Over the next six months, 430 patients were admitted to the hospital: 215 patients were put in rooms with copper bed rails and 215 patients were put in rooms with plastic bed rails. Dr. West counted the number of patients in each type of room who got new infections while they were in the hospital.

elements.text: Cooper noticed that some of the footballs his team used during practice were not fully inflated. He wondered whether fully inflated footballs would travel farther than footballs with a lower air pressure.

To find out, Cooper collected 20 standard footballs. He fully inflated ten of them to an air pressure of 13 pounds per square inch. He inflated the remaining ten to an air pressure of 10 pounds per square inch. Cooper used a football launcher to launch a ball across a football field. He measured the distance the football traveled and then launched the next ball. Cooper repeated this with all 20 balls.

elements.text: Marie liked to make guacamole, but she could often find only unripe avocados at the grocery store. In biology class, Marie learned that ripe fruits produce a gas called ethylene that can cause other fruits to ripen. Marie wondered whether storing ripe bananas with unripe avocados would make the avocados ripen faster.

Marie prepared four paper bags with five unripe avocados in each bag. She added one ripe banana to two of the bags and no bananas to the remaining two bags. Then, Marie sealed all four bags. After three days, she opened each bag and counted the number of ripe avocados in each bag.

elements.text: Lena was learning to bake bread at home. Her first few batches of dough did not rise, or expand, as much as they should have. Lena's mother noted that the kitchen was cold and suggested that the dough might not be warm enough to rise.

Lena decided to test her mother's suggestion. She made a large batch of dough and divided it into six equal-sized balls. Then, she put each ball into a bowl. She left three bowls on the counter in the kitchen, where the temperature was 63°F. She left the other three bowls on her desk in her upstairs bedroom, where the temperature was 80°F. After one hour, Lena measured the size of each dough ball.

He recorded how many days it took each nail to become completely covered in rust. lessons.name: Understand an experimental protocol about plant growth

pieces.text: The instructions for how to carry out a science experiment can be found in an

. An experimental protocol often includes the list of materials you need for the experiment. The protocol also includes the procedure, which is a list of steps for carrying out the experiment. Some experimental protocols include data tables for recording the results of the experiment.

header.text: The experimental protocol below is for an experiment investigating tomato plant growth. Read through the experimental protocol, then answer the question below.

elements.text: Pour the soil into the large plastic container and add water until the soil is moist.
Fill the pots with the moistened soil. Label each pot with a number from 1 through 10.
Plant one tomato plant in each pot.
In pots 6 through 10, add two earthworms just beneath the soil surface.
Place all of the pots next to each other in a warm, sunny area.
Once a day, give each plant four ounces of water.
After three months, count the number of tomatoes on each plant.
Record your results in the following tables.

content.text: Plants grown in soil without earthworms
Plants grown in soil with earthworms

contents.text: In this experiment, the independent variable is the amount of time each beaker is under a heat lamp. The amount of time spent under a heat lamp may affect the rate of evaporation, or how quickly the water evaporates.
The more quickly the water evaporates, the less water will be remaining after three days. The water remaining after three days is the dependent variable.

header.text: So, the experiment can answer this question:

content.text: Does the amount of time under a heat lamp affect the rate of evaporation?

content.text: Does the amount of time under a heat lamp affect the water temperature?

content.text: Does the salinity of water affect the rate of evaporation?

explanationText.text: In this experiment, all the beakers are filled with tap water. So, this experiment does not test the effect of salinity.

contents.text: In this experiment, the independent variable is the salinity of the water. The salinity of the water may affect the rate of evaporation, or how quickly the water evaporates.
The more quickly the water evaporates, the less water will remain after three days. The water remaining after three days is the dependent variable.

header.text: So, the experiment can answer this question:

content.text: Does the salinity of the water affect the rate of evaporation?

header.text: The experiment cannot answer these questions:

content.text: Does the temperature of the water affect the rate of evaporation?

explanationText.text: In this experiment, the temperature of the water in each beaker is the same. So, this experiment does not test the effect of temperature.

content.text: Does the size of the beaker affect the rate of evaporation?

explanationText.text: In this experiment, the beakers are identical, or the same. So, this experiment does not test the effect of using beakers of different sizes.
